claims.text: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (this edition spells it Spake) is a philosophical book by Friedrich Nietzsche, in the form of speeches and parables by an invented prophet, Zarathustra, who comes down from the mountains to teach people.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: In the Prologue, we see Zarathustra coming down to teach the people the message that god is dead and that man is to be overcome.

claims.text: It was written in bursts in 1883 and early 1884: Part I took about ten days in January 1883, Part II came in June and Part III in November.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: Part I was written in only about ten days, in January 1883. In February, Wagner died, yielding yet another blow to Nietzsche. Part II was written in June 1883 and Part III, in November.

claims.text: The fourth part was written in January 1884 and shown only to a small group. It was thought too blasphemous to publish in Nietzsche's lifetime, so the four parts first appeared together in 1892.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: Part IV, written in January 1884, was circulated to only a small group and not published during Nietzsche's lifetime. It was viewed as too blasphemous.

items.heading: A world in which belief in God is fading

claims.text: The book assumes that the traditional Christian picture of the world has lost its hold on educated Europeans. Zarathustra's first message to the crowd is that God is dead and that humanity must be overcome, and the crowd does not understand him.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: In the Prologue, we see Zarathustra coming down to teach the people the message that god is dead and that man is to be overcome.

claims.text: In the Second Part, Zarathustra says that where people once looked to God, they should now look to the overman, a figure standing for human destiny.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: When we look into the sea (nature), we should see overman (human destiny) and not god.

items.heading: A year of heartbreak and isolation

claims.text: In spring 1882 Nietzsche met Lou Salomé, a young Russian woman, in Rome. His hope of spending the summer with her and his friend Paul Rée, a philosopher, was ended by interference from his mother and sister Elisabeth.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: Nietzsche's hopes of spending an extended period of time (the summer of 1882) with Lou and Paul Ree were crushed by the manipulations of his mother and sister, Elizabeth.

claims.text: Nietzsche wrote bitter letters to both friends and felt regret and guilt afterwards. He was alienated from almost everyone he knew, and friends in Basel feared he might be suicidal.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: Nietzsche allowed his jealousy to pour forth and wrote some terrible letters to his two formerly-best friends, also slandering them to other friends.

claims.text: The writing of Zarathustra is described as the healing process that brought him out of this dark period.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: In many respects, the writing of Zarathustra was the healing process that brought Nietzsche out of this darkness.

items.heading: A wandering writer in the Alps and Italy

claims.text: From 1881 to 1888 Nietzsche spent his summers in Sils Maria, a high Swiss Alpine village, except in 1882. The second part of Zarathustra and a draft of the third were written there in summer 1883.

citations.title: Splendid Isolation: Nietzsche At Sils Maria
citations.quote: Nietzsche spent summers in Sils Maria, a village in the 2000-metre high Engadine Valley, surrounded by the Swiss Alps.

citations.title: The following summers: 1884-1888
citations.quote: the 2nd and the draft for the 3rd book of “Thus spoke Zarathustra” in the summer of 1883

claims.text: He wrote for readers who did not yet exist: he is described as ahead of his time and writing for people who do not yet live. That helps explain why the book was shown to so few people at first.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: He is, after all, ahead of his time and writes for people who do not yet live.

claims.text: Wagner, the composer who had been Nietzsche's early idol, died in February 1883, between the writing of Parts I and II. It was another blow to Nietzsche at the time.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: In February, Wagner died, yielding yet another blow to Nietzsche.

claims.text: Lou sought intellectual companionship rather than love, and went off with Rée instead, living with him for several years. Nietzsche's disappointment is the personal backdrop to the book.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: Lou went off with Ree alone and wound up living with him for several years.

claims.text: The book picks up themes from Nietzsche's previous book, The Gay Science (1882), including its talk of God's death. Part II returns to and amplifies those themes.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: An entire year stands between the publication of The Gay Science and the writing of Part I, Thus Spoke Zarathustra.

claims.text: The overman is Zarathustra's name for the human destiny that should replace God as the thing people look toward. Some translators render it Superman, as this edition does.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: When we look into the sea (nature), we should see overman (human destiny) and not god.

claims.text: The idea that all events return again and again came to Nietzsche in his first summer at Sils Maria in 1881, and it runs through every book he wrote afterwards.

citations.title: Splendid Isolation: Nietzsche At Sils Maria
citations.quote: the insight that would permeate every book that followed: that of the Eternal Return.

claims.text: In Part I, the speech "On the Thousand and One Goals" introduces the will to power as the creative drive behind people's tables of good and evil, tied to self-overcoming. It is not simply about dominating others.

citations.title: Reading Notes for Nietzsche
citations.quote: Nietzsche introduces his concept of the will to power in the context of self-overcoming as the creative activity behind our "tablets" of our good.
